articles.title: Railroads, coal towns, and lives along the New River
articles.text: The gorge preserves the connected histories of Indigenous communities, settlers, railroad workers, miners, and timber workers. Rail transport helped coal and logging towns grow, while later industrial decline left places such as Thurmond as evidence of those changing economies. Oral histories and surviving town sites help explain the people behind the industrial landscape.
articles.evidence: the ensuing boom and bust of the coal mining and logging industries

pageMetadata.title: History & Culture - New River Gorge National Park & Preserve

articles.title: A gorge that connects and divides habitats
articles.text: The New River cuts through Appalachian rock formations and a varied forest landscape. Riverbanks, cliffs, plateaus, and sheltered coves create different habitats within the gorge. NPS describes the river corridor as a possible route for southern species moving into West Virginia, while the gorge can also limit some species' movement from east to west.
articles.evidence: provides a geographical barrier that limits the east-west distribution of other species

pageMetadata.title: Nature & Science - New River Gorge National Park & Preserve

articles.title: Indigenous life before written accounts
articles.text: Archaeological evidence in the New River Gorge reaches far earlier than European written accounts. Clovis points document early hunting communities; later pottery, tools, seeds, and village remains show farming settlements linked by trails. These places preserve a long sequence of Indigenous life, and leaving artifacts undisturbed protects the context needed to understand it.
articles.evidence: The oldest artifacts from New River Gorge are Clovis points.

articles.title: Canal, railway, and the campaign to preserve a valley
articles.text: The Ohio & Erie Canal and Valley Railway strengthened connections between valley farms and the growing cities of Cleveland and Akron. The valley also became a place for urban residents to spend leisure time. In the twentieth century, residents and political leaders pushed for federal protection as suburban development threatened its landscape.
articles.evidence: Local residents and political leaders worked to stop suburban development that threatened the valley.

pageMetadata.title: History & Culture - Cuyahoga Valley National Park

articles.title: Habitats along the crooked river
articles.text: Riverbank habitat, deciduous forest, wetlands, working farmland, and old fields form Cuyahoga Valley's habitat mosaic. The park sits where the Appalachian Plateau meets the Central Lowlands, in terrain reshaped by repeated glaciations. Steep ravines carry tributaries from the uplands toward the Cuyahoga River.
articles.evidence: the Appalachian Plateau and the Central Lowlands

pageMetadata.title: Nature & Science - Cuyahoga Valley National Park

articles.title: Native communities across generations
articles.text: Indigenous people in the valley adapted from mobile hunting to seasonal camps and more settled communities, drawing food and materials from forests and waterways. Warfare and displacement profoundly changed those communities. Native people continue to live in the Cleveland region, maintain cultural traditions, and participate in the park's relationships with associated Tribes.
articles.evidence: Those who live here now work together to preserve and celebrate their cultures.

history.event: Enabling legislation authorized Cuyahoga Valley National Recreation Area under Public Law 93-555.

pageMetadata.title: Press Kit - Cuyahoga Valley National Park

articles.title: Civic groups and the creation of Acadia
articles.text: Local improvement groups built trails and responded to development pressures as tourism grew around Mount Desert Island. Conservation organizations and private donors then assembled land for public protection. The park developed through the Sieur de Monts, Lafayette, and Acadia names; NPS also acknowledges that this conservation history rests on Indigenous displacement.
articles.evidence: these groups built an island wide trail system

articles.title: Rocky coast, forest transition, and migration
articles.text: Acadia combines rocky shorelines and exposed summits with lakes, streams, wetlands, forests, and meadows. Its position between northern and southern forest regions places some plant communities near the edges of their ranges. The park also provides resting and feeding habitat for migrating birds and bats along the Atlantic flyway.
articles.evidence: Acadia is within the transition zone between southern and northern forests

articles.title: Acadia in the Wabanaki homeland
articles.text: Acadia remains part of the homeland of Wabanaki peoples, including Maliseet, Mi'kmaq, Passamaquoddy, and Penobscot communities. Generations traveled by land and birchbark canoe, gathering food and maintaining connections around Mount Desert Island. Tribal governments continue relationships with the park, and work on traditional plant gathering supports renewed cultural practices in these places.
articles.evidence: Tribal governments have a government-to-government relationship with Acadia National Park.

history.event: President Woodrow Wilson created Sieur de Monts National Monument following land donations for federal protection.
history.evidence: in 1916 President Wilson announced the creation of Sieur de Monts National Monument

history.event: Lafayette National Park was established, and George B. Dorr became its first superintendent.
The name Acadia National Park was adopted when Congress authorized acceptance of land on the Schoodic Peninsula.

articles.title: The Yosemite Grant and the later national park
articles.text: The Yosemite Grant protected Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove under California's administration before the surrounding national park was created. The grant lands joined the federal park later. These were separate stages in Yosemite's protection, so the national park designation date does not mark the beginning of all public protection here.
articles.evidence: The Grant was administered by the State of California until 1906

pageMetadata.title: Yosemite National Park Celebrates 120th Birthday on October 1

articles.title: Granite, uplift, and ice
articles.text: Yosemite's landscape records both the formation of granitic rocks and their later exposure and erosion. Uplift and tilting helped build the Sierra Nevada, while glaciers, flowing water, and changing temperatures shaped the rock into valleys, domes, cliffs, and waterfalls. Today's landmarks preserve evidence of several interacting geological processes.
articles.evidence: Later came uplift, erosion, and glaciation of the rocks

articles.title: Surviving communities and ancestral connections
articles.text: Some Ahwahneechee returned to Yosemite Valley and rebuilt small communities, joined by survivors from other Tribes. NPS identifies seven traditionally associated Tribes and groups with ancestral connections to the park, including Southern Sierra Miwuk, Paiute, Mono, Chukchansi, and Me-Wuk communities. Those connections continue through the park's work with associated Tribes today.
articles.evidence: Some Ahwahneechee slowly returned and established small communities in the Valley.

history.event: President Abraham Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant, setting aside Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove for public use and recreation under California's administration.

articles.title: From Mukuntuweap to Zion National Park
articles.text: Federal protection began with Mukuntuweap National Monument. The monument was later enlarged and renamed Zion before receiving national park status. A separate neighboring Zion National Monument was subsequently created and eventually combined with the park. These changes reflect several stages of protection rather than a single founding event.
articles.evidence: The park and monument were combined by an Act of Congress

pageMetadata.title: Biophysical Description of Zion National Park
pageMetadata.basis: Summary of a monitoring plan published in 2004; used here for historical events only.

articles.title: Water and elevation create Zion's habitats
articles.text: Zion's plateaus and sandstone canyons support desert, riverbank, pinyon-juniper, and conifer woodland communities. Springs and seeps sustain hanging gardens on canyon walls. Differences in elevation and the meeting of neighboring ecological regions help explain why dry slopes, lush river corridors, and cooler forests occur close together.
articles.evidence: Desert, riparian (river bank), pinyon-juniper, and conifer woodland communities

articles.title: Communities and living knowledge in Zion
articles.text: Zion's archaeological record includes homes and communities associated with Archaic peoples, Ancestral Puebloans, and Southern Paiute people. Descendant communities remain in the Great Basin and Colorado Plateau. Their family records and oral traditions continue to contribute to understanding the canyon's human history alongside the material evidence preserved in the park.
articles.evidence: These communities' descendants still live in the Great Basin and Colorado Plateau

history.event: A presidential proclamation established Mukuntuweap National Monument, protecting the area that became Zion National Park.

articles.title: A refuge and a forest worth protecting
articles.text: Congaree's floodplain offered refuge to enslaved people who escaped plantations and built lives in the woods. Later, commercial logging removed old cypress before difficult access made operations unprofitable. Harry Hampton and subsequent conservation advocates helped turn renewed logging threats into a campaign for federal protection of the remaining forest.
articles.evidence: served as a refuge

pageMetadata.title: People in the Floodplain
pageMetadata.section: A Refuge from Slavery; Champions Begin to Fall; Congaree Action Now

articles.title: Flood and fire shape different forests
articles.text: Floodwaters from the Congaree and Wateree Rivers spread sediment and nutrients through the bottomland forest. Small elevation differences help determine where wetlands, sloughs, oxbow lakes, and different tree communities occur. On higher ground, fire helps maintain upland pine forest, making both flooding and burning important ecological processes in the park.
articles.evidence: defined by the presence of both flood and flame

articles.title: The Congaree name and earlier floodplain communities
articles.text: The park and river take their name from the Congaree people of this region. Archaeological evidence documents earlier communities that moved from temporary camps toward villages and agriculture. The floodplain's Indigenous history therefore extends beyond the colonial accounts that recorded the Congaree name.
articles.evidence: named for the Congaree people who once lived in this region

history.event: Commercial logging operations described in the park's floodplain history had ceased after extraction proved difficult and costly.
Congaree Swamp National Monument was authorized to protect the floodplain forest.

articles.title: From Mound City monument to a wider protected landscape
articles.text: The park began as Mound City Group National Monument. Later legislation added land at Hopeton and led to investigation of other earthwork sites. The national historical park designation expanded protection to additional complexes, preserving a wider record of the ceremonial and social traditions represented by these earthworks.
articles.evidence: evolved in part from the former Mound City Group National Monument

pageMetadata.title: History & Culture - Hopewell Culture National Historical Park

articles.title: Restoring habitat around the earthworks
articles.text: Hopewell Culture's protected sites contain deciduous woods, former agricultural fields, river corridors, grasslands, and wetlands. Staff and volunteers monitor native and invasive species across these habitats. Restoration of native grasses and flowering plants aims to improve conditions for birds that nest in grasslands.
articles.evidence: Restoration efforts are ongoing for native grasses and forbs

pageMetadata.title: Nature & Science - Hopewell Culture National Historical Park

articles.title: What the name Hopewell represents
articles.text: Native people built the monumental geometric earthworks of the Scioto Valley. The archaeological label Hopewell comes from a later landowner, rather than the builders' own name or the name of a Tribe. Forced removal of Ohio's Tribal Nations preceded early archaeological investigations, which took place without Indigenous participation.
articles.evidence: "Hopewell" is not the name of any American Indian tribe.

articles.title: Routes, ranches, and surviving historic places
articles.text: The Guadalupe Mountains preserve histories of Mescalero Apache people, conflict with soldiers, overland mail, and ranching. The Frijole and Williams ranch sites and the Pinery Station ruins retain evidence of different periods of settlement and travel. Their buildings and archaeological remains help explain human life in this mountain and desert landscape.
articles.evidence: preserved at the Frijole and Williams Ranches, and at the ruins of the Pinery Station

pageMetadata.title: History & Culture - Guadalupe Mountains National Park

articles.title: An exposed fossil reef in a desert mountain range
articles.text: The Guadalupe Mountains expose part of a marine reef formed in a Permian tropical sea. Sponges, algae, and other organisms contributed limestone material as the reef grew. Burial under sediments and salts preserved it before later uplift exposed the rocks, allowing scientists to examine an ancient marine environment within today's desert landscape.
articles.evidence: until uplift exposed massive portions of it

pageMetadata.title: Nature & Science - Guadalupe Mountains National Park

articles.title: Mescalero Apache relationships with the Guadalupes
articles.text: Mescalero Apache people used the mountains' animals and plants through seasonal movement, with agave important for food, fiber, and cultural practices. Settler expansion and military conflict drove many from the Guadalupes. NPS describes the mountains as a continuing cultural and spiritual sanctuary for Mescalero Apache people.
articles.evidence: an important cultural and spiritual sanctuary for the Mescalero Apaches

history.event: An early landowner began advocating national park status for the Guadalupe Mountains.
history.evidence: Beginning in 1925 one landowner was an early advocate

history.event: Guadalupe Mountains National Park was formally established, six years after congressional authorization.
history.evidence: on September 30, 1972, Guadalupe Mountains National Park was formally established
